items.headline: Alibaba previews Qwen3.8 at 2.4 trillion parameters and promises an open-weight release
items.diff_narrative: The slate turns over completely: not one of yesterday's five substantive storylines carries into today, not one of today's five resumes a thread from the days behind it, and only the events roll survives the cut. What does cross over is a name rather than a story. Claude Fable 5 was yesterday's subject — kept in Max and Team Premium at 50% of limits from July 20, with Pro and Team Standard dropped to a one-time $100 credit and then API rates — and today it reappears as somebody else's measuring stick, with Alibaba claiming Qwen3.8 sits second only to Fable 5 among generally available systems. The open-weight axis also changes register. Yesterday it was an execution result: Colibri streaming GLM-5.2's 744 billion parameters off disk so an existing model became reachable on 25GB of RAM with no GPU. Today it is an announcement — 2.4 trillion parameters, the first Qwen multimodal model above the trillion-parameter line, taking images, video and documents, with access starting proprietary through Alibaba's Token Plan, Qoder and QoderWork at a tenth of standard pricing and the weights promised but undated. No benchmark results back either the Fable 5 comparison or the claimed gain over Qwen3.7-Max, which leaves today's entry as a commitment where yesterday's was a running artifact, and puts it three days behind Moonshot's 2.8-trillion-parameter Kimi K3 — the two largest announced open-weight models in the world arriving inside one week, both Chinese.

items.headline: A botnet called NadMesh hunts exposed Ollama, ComfyUI and Langflow instances for cloud credentials
items.diff_narrative: The security slot holds its position and flips altitude, from the weights to the open ports. Yesterday's entry was OpenAI's GPT-Red, adversarial self-play at the frontier: an attacker model reaching an 84% success rate on novel indirect prompt injections against GPT-5.1 where human red teamers managed 13%, fed back into six times fewer direct-injection failures in GPT-5.6 Sol. Today's is the unglamorous other end of the same problem. QiAnXin's XLab describes NadMesh scanning specifically for self-hosted AI infrastructure — ComfyUI, Ollama, n8n, Open WebUI, Langflow, Gradio — and taking credentials rather than compute: cloud keys out of environment variables, Kubernetes service-account tokens, the contents of ~/.aws/config, .env and ~/.docker/config.json, plus whatever MCP tools the host can call. Initial access is ordinary misconfiguration rather than anything AI-specific, with Docker API remote code execution at 30.31% of observed traffic, Jenkins script-console execution at 22.28%, weak telnet passwords at 10.36% and Redis at 8.29%. The evidentiary posture inverts as well: yesterday's figures were vendor-published and internally coherent, while today's headline numbers come from the operator's own dashboard — 3,811 unique AWS keys, 47 credential hauls across its last 100 records — and the entry says plainly they cannot be trusted, since a 17,700 total-deploy counter sits above a funnel claiming 95,700 in the preceding 24 hours. The sharpest pairing is with yesterday's Colibri: the same class of self-hosted tooling that read as a capability win one day is an enumerated attack surface the next, with ports 8188, 11434, 7860 and 5678 as the remediation list.

items.headline: Moonshine Micro fits detection, speech recognition and text-to-speech into 470KB of RAM on an 80-cent microcontroller
items.diff_narrative: Local inference keeps a slot across both days and swaps ends of the scale. Yesterday Colibri argued the ceiling: 744 billion parameters, a roughly 370GB int4 container on disk, 19,456 routed experts streaming under an LRU cache, a 25GB RAM floor, and 0.05 to 0.1 tokens per second as the bill — frontier scale bought with wall-clock time. Today Moonshine Micro argues the floor: voice-activity detection, speech recognition and neural text-to-speech together in about 468 KiB of SRAM and near 3.6 MiB of flash on an RP2350 retailing around 80 cents, MIT-licensed, roughly 0.7 to 1.0 seconds from speech in to speech out on TensorFlow Lite Micro. Both entries buy locality by surrendering something, and the currency is what separates them — Colibri gives up latency to keep a frontier model's full capability, Moonshine gives up capability to keep latency, recognizing about 50 custom words or phrases retrainable to an application's own vocabulary. The demo makes the case in a way yesterday's memory-hierarchy accounting could not: a user configures a wifi connection entirely by voice, with no cloud round trip, no API key and no account. Read against NadMesh in the same slate, the two local-inference entries also split on exposure — one is a workstation holding cloud credentials while listening on an open port, the other is a device with nothing to steal and nowhere to phone home.

items.headline: A ten-page prompt gets GPT-5.6 to close an oracle-complexity gap that had stood since 1996
items.diff_narrative: A research slot appears that yesterday's slate did not have at all, and it lands as the counterweight to yesterday's GPT-Red. Both describe a model doing work that used to require people, but they are measured in opposite units. GPT-Red arrived as rates across scenarios — 84% against 13%, a 0.05% failure rate, above 97% on indirect-injection benchmarks — every figure published by the vendor whose model the work hardens. Today's result is a single object anyone can check: Phillip Kerger's July 14 proof that deterministic value-only minimization of a convex Lipschitz function over a d-dimensional Euclidean ball requires Omega(d^2 / log(d+1)) queries at accuracy Theta(d^-1/2), closing to polylogarithmic factors a gap open since 1996 between the known Omega(d) lower bound and Protasov's O(d^2 log^2 d) method, with a Lean formalization generated alongside it. The provenance that surfaced on July 18 is the substance — roughly a year of the author's own work on the problem, unsuccessful attempts with GPT-5.4 and GPT-5.5, then a prompt running about ten pages that laid out the reasonable approaches from the literature. Today's entry also demotes a larger claim by sitting next to it: OpenAI's Cycle Double Cover announcement ran 64 parallel agents and remains unformalized and un-peer-reviewed, while this one produced a machine-checkable artifact with a single named human carrying responsibility for it.

items.headline: DeepSeek lines up a second raise in two months at a $74 billion valuation and weighs a STAR Market listing
items.diff_narrative: The funding slot survives the turnover and reverses both its stage and its geography. Yesterday it was a first institutional round for a company with no revenue to report — Walden Robotics leaving stealth on a $300 million seed at a $1.1 billion valuation, co-led by Toyota, its credibility resting on robots already doing production work in a North American plant since February 2026. Today it is a company that spent years refusing outside capital: DeepSeek preparing a raise at roughly 500 billion yuan, about $74 billion, seeking as much as 50 billion, only weeks after a June round that took in about $7.4 billion at a post-money valuation near 450 billion yuan — with early deliberations under way on a Shanghai STAR Market listing and an internal target of filing this year. The cap tables encode the difference. Walden's was prospective customers: a manufacturer, an aerospace prime, a chip vendor and a warehouse REIT's venture arm. DeepSeek's June register is founder Liang Wenfeng committing 20 billion yuan personally, Tencent at 10 billion and battery maker CATL at 5 billion as the largest external holders, with China's state AI investment fund holding the only outside board voting rights. Yesterday's round bought a company its first outside money; today's replaces the High-Flyer self-funding that let DeepSeek ship cheap open-weight models without answering to a quarterly clock. It also rhymes with today's Alibaba entry, where Moonshot is reported at roughly $300 million in annual recurring revenue with an IPO targeted inside six months — two Chinese labs on listing timetables in one slate, while their model announcements race each other by three days.

items.headline: AI events to plan around now: the AGI Summit closes today and AMD Advancing AI is full in person
items.diff_narrative: The one genuine continuation, and the clock moved on two fronts. The AGI Summit crosses from the middle of its run to its closing day: yesterday it was July 18-19 with 7 AM doors and a speaker roster to weigh, today it is July 19 alone, 9 AM to 5 PM at the Palace of Fine Arts on Lyon Street, with walk-up tickets from $199 and the $49 student rate on a valid .edu address as the only thing left to decide. WAIC keeps its July 20 close but is now tomorrow rather than a date on the horizon. The substantive state change is AMD's Advancing AI: yesterday's note was that registration closes before the July 22 opening, and today in-person registration is full, so the route in is Lisa Su's keynote at 9:30 AM PT on July 23, livestreamed on AMD's YouTube channel, with the more than 100 breakouts, tech talks and workshops around it reserved for those already holding a badge — a trip across town becomes a browser tab. Hot Chips keeps its July 31 early-rate cutoff and gains the exact terms, 11:59 PM PDT that Friday with cancellations accepted until August 19. The early-August security block resolves from one undifferentiated August 1-6 Las Vegas stretch into separable commitments: Black Hat at Mandalay Bay August 1-6, Trainings August 1-4 and Briefings August 5-6 with its AI Summit on August 4, then DEF CON 34 August 6-9 where the AI Village runs demos, capture-the-flag and a new poster track on adversarial attacks against agents, then SecurityWeek's AI Risk Summit at Half Moon Bay August 11-12, which gains the Ritz-Carlton as its venue. Several entries acquire the details you can only act on once they exist — the AI Tinkerers meetup pins to August 9, 6 to 9 PM at Founders Inc; Zenity's series pins to London October 8 and New York October 21; the AI Infra Summit gains $1,497 full access, roughly 8,000 attendees, 400-plus speakers and complimentary passes for enterprise technologists; SANS adds a November 2-3 Arlington summit at $525 in person with live-online attendance free, a hotel-rate deadline of October 9 and refunds until October 14. NVIDIA's GTC joins the roll only to mark its absence, not returning to San Jose until March 15-18, 2027.
